rows.description: You want them only yours and feel entitled to know everything. Wise: see this as fear, not love, and see them as a separate person. Harmful: controlling clothes, contacts or location.
Their control is framed as love, and you slowly shrink your world. Wise: recognise the pattern, talk to a trusted friend or counsellor, and do not accept it as normal. It is not your fault.
My stomach twists when she laughs with the new girl. I want to say I miss her, not sulk or steal her back. Sulking and spreading rumours about the newcomer only pushes her further away.

My friend acts cold since I made a new friend, and I feel guilty and cornered. Kind action: reassure her, keep our special time, and invite her in. Dropping the new friend or hiding her is not needed.

Different cities or colleges mean less contact and you feel a quiet loss. Wise: accept friendships change, reach out without keeping score, and let some stay smaller. Immature: sulking or cutting them off first.
A friend is pulling back and you wonder what you did. Wise: ask once, kindly, and accept if they need space. Harmful: guilt trips or demanding equal effort.

I peek during hide and seek or move my counter to win. I feel excited and a bit guilty. Winning feels huge at this age. A wise adult says "the game is only fun if it is fair", not "you are a cheater".
My friend moved his piece when I was not looking. I feel furious and say "cheater!" A wise action is to say "that is not fair, play again properly". Walking away is also fine if he keeps doing it.

My neighbour's noise, parking, or garbage keeps annoying me and my irritation has built up. I speak to them calmly before it explodes, propose a specific fix, and use society rules only if talking fails.

A neighbour is shouting at me over a small matter and I feel my own temper rising. I stay calm, listen, offer to resolve it later, and avoid an audience; involving elders or the society committee helps if it escalates.

I roll my eyes and mock my partner's habits, feeling superior and tired. Contempt is the most corrosive habit in marriage; the wise move is to name the hurt underneath and ask for what I need, not score points.

I am being sneered at or talked down to by my partner, and I feel small and unsafe to speak. It is not my fault. I calmly name the pattern, ask for respect, and seek counselling if it continues; I avoid answering contempt with contempt.
